parties:
Province Of East Pakistan (Now Bangladesh)
Vs.
Syeduddin Ahmed
full_judgment:
2. Bangladesh is the appellant. The respondent as plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration of his title to the suit land alleging, inter alia, that he was alloted 5 acres of Govt. Khas land from mouza Telikhali in 1958. The Settlement was made in Settlement case No.3 of 1958-59. It was duly approved by the Additional Collector and since then the plaintiff has been in possession of the said land. In 1962 the Board of Revenue, it is alleged, by an order dated 3-10-61 cancelled the settlement. Hence the suit. 

 3. The appellant contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the respondent or the members of his family were not cultivators and he was therefore, not entitled to settlement of Government khas lands under the rules. The Board of Revenue was justified in cancelling the settlement. 

 11. An appeal was preferred and it was disposed of by the Secretary, Revenue Department by its order dated 7-7-62. It was considered that the appellants were not entitled to settlement of the Government khas land and as such the settlement with them were not legal "though some of the petitioners claim that kabuliyats for the lands executed by them have been accepted by the Government thereby establishing a relationship of landlord and tenant between them and the Government, that stand is not correct because the Kabuliyats were not accepted by the Collector or an authorised agent of the case" and the order was passed. "The appeals are therefore failed on merit". Then the last paragraph mentioned: "Again, the orders for settlement of lands by the Collector in these were cancelled under Orders of the Governor and not under any order of the Board of Revenue and as such, no appeal is actually maintainable. The result is that the appeal petitions fail." 

 13. It lays down the rule of priority as to who will get preference to get Government khas land: In this case the main objection of the Government is that the plaintiff was not a bonafide, cultivator. It was alleged in the order of cancellation that the plaintiff got the settlement by exercising "undue influence". Neither he was heard nor his appeal was disposed of after giving him any hearing. So the question of undue influence has not been substantiated. In the suit the plaintiff examined witnesses but the Government did not. Therefore the very basis that the plaintiff obtained settlement by .exercising undue influence appears to be lacking. 

 "Provided further that in making settlement of any cultivable land preference shall be given to an applicant for settlement who cultivates land by himself or by the members of his family". Section 78 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act gives the rule making power and clause(zt) provides for the rules for settlement of lands referred to in section 76. In section 82 'bonafide cultivator' is defined for the purpose of part V means "a person who cultivates lands by himself or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of servants or labourers or with the aid of partners or bargadars, and also includes on agricultural labourer;". The learned Additional Attorney General is correct in contending that this definition in section 82 in only for the purpose of that part and this definition is wider then the persons meant by the bonafide cultivator in rule 63(3). That rule is to be taken as principle to be followed in the matter of settlement of the Government khas land and it mentioned 'bonafide cultivator' and includes the "members of the family of such cultivator who will cultivate the land himself or get them cultivated by members of his own family". In other words, it excludes the servants or labourers or partners or bargadars or cultivator labourer. The idea is plain, namely, Government land should be settled with the bonafide cultivator or a member of the family of bonafide cultivator. The emphasis is on "who will cultivate the land himself or get them cultivated by the members of his own family". Ext.3 the kabuliat exactly speaks in the same terms: "I shall cultivate land myself or with the members of my family ". When in the kabuliyat members of the family are included, it is difficult to appreciate the judgment of the trial court when the evidence of P.W.3 Fazlul Hoque was brushed aside by observing: "I decide that Fazlul Huq simply looks after and manages the suit property under the plaintiff" and concluded that "Fazlul Huq the nephew of the plaintiff though allegedly resides with his maternal uncle the plaintiff cannot be member of his family". To say the least, those who are conversant with the family condition of our villages would not consider the assertion of P.W.3 Fazlul Hoque as something improbable when he says that he resides in the plaintiff's house and manages his property and also ploughs land. 

 18. Thus it is clear that the expression `family' is to be understood in the light of the given enactment. In so far settlement of the khas land is concerned the expression 'Family' has not been used in definitive sense; the emphasis is only on the point that the land should be cultivated by himself or by member of the family. Evidence was led by the plaintiff that his nephew ploughed the land who resided with him. This evidence was not rebutted. Since this condition is satisfied it cannot be said that the plaintiff respondent did not answer the description of the person to whom settlement could be made.
